title: Why Does Salt Melt Ice?
description:
Salt melts ice, but how? At 0 °C, ice and water trade molecules at the same rate, so nothing seems to change. Dissolved salt ions crowd the water next to the ice, so fewer water molecules stick, while melting goes on at nearly the same rate: the ice shrinks. Melting takes heat, so salty ice water cools itself below zero, down toward about −21 °C with enough table salt. That is how ice cream in a bag works, why road salt gets too slow below about −9 °C, and how a pinch of salt lets you lift an ice cube with a thread.

subtitles: This ice cube is hanging from a thread.
No knot, no glue.
Just a pinch of salt, and a couple of minutes.
Salt melts ice.
Most people know that.
But salt also makes ice water colder than zero.
To see how, we have to watch the molecules.
Here is ice sitting in water, at 0 °C.
Nothing seems to happen.
But at the surface, the molecules never stop moving.
Some break free from the ice and join the water.
Others stick back on.
At zero degrees, both happen at the same rate, so the ice neither grows nor shrinks.
Chemists call this a dynamic equilibrium.
Busy, but balanced.
Warm it a little, and more molecules break free.
Cool it a little, and more stick.
Now add salt.
In water, it splits into two kinds of ions, sodium and chloride.
The ions crowd in among the water molecules next to the ice.
They do not fit into the ice crystal, so they stay in the water.
Fewer water molecules reach the ice each second, so fewer stick.
But melting goes on at nearly the same rate.
Melting wins, and the ice shrinks.
To balance it again, you have to cool it below zero.
That is the new freezing point.
Seawater has about 3.5 % salt.
It freezes at about −1.9 °C.
More salt, lower freezing point.
Mostly, what matters is how many particles you dissolve.
But melting always takes heat.
Where does it come from?
Nobody is supplying any.
So the ice and the water around it give up their own heat.
The whole mix cools below zero, and keeps melting until it reaches the new freezing point.
That is how you make ice cream in a bag.
Ice, salt, and a lot of shaking.
With enough table salt, the mix can get down toward −21 °C.
That is as cold as salt water can get and still stay liquid.
Which explains a winter problem.
On a road at −3 °C, salt works well.
But the colder it gets, the less ice each handful can melt, and the slower it works.
Near −1 °C, a kilo of salt can melt about 46 kg of ice.
Near −7 °C, only about nine.
Below about −9 °C, road crews usually find plain rock salt too slow.
Then they switch to liquid de-icers, or to chemicals that work at colder temperatures.
And the thread?
Same physics, on a tiny scale.
Without salt, nothing happens.
The ice and the thin film of water both sit at zero.
Salt melts a thin layer of ice around the thread, and that melting pulls heat out of the cube.
The cube gets colder than zero.
The meltwater dilutes the salt, and the cold cube freezes the water around the thread again.
With the thread inside.
Lift, and the cube comes with it.
So salt does not heat the ice.
It tips a balance.
Fewer molecules freeze, about the same number melt, and the ice pays for its own melting with heat.
Try the thread trick tonight, and tell me how many cubes you lifted at once.
